title: Waitrose to expand digital broadcasting after festive ad launch wins 2m views
summary:
Chief executive of supermarket says it is considering new projects after success of Dish podcast and YouTube channel

Waitrose is to expand its digital broadcasting portfolio after…

blocks.text: Waitrose is to expand its digital broadcasting portfolio after this year’s Christmas ad launch with Keira Knightley attracted more that 2 million viewers.

“There are not many brands that would command an appointment of you for six minutes on ITV to launch their Christmas ad and have 2.3 million people show up to watch,” said the supermarket’s chief executive, Tom Denyard.

Showing the Guardian around Waitrose’s latest shop which opened in the wealthy Greater Manchester neighbourhood of Hale Barns last week, he said the company was looking at more digital ideas. “We would be daft not to think about that as an opportunity,” he said.

Waitrose is already a serious digital player with the Dish podcast, hosted by the DJ Nick Grimshaw and the chef Angela Hartnett, which has been downloaded more than 1.3bn times. It says its social media following has risen 8% year on year and fans spent more than 1m hours watching its YouTube channel in the last 12 months, double the previous year.

It launched a weekly recipe and tutorials series, Let’s Cook, this summer and has taken Dish live, selling more than 2,000 tickets for an event at the Royal Opera House. It also has a growing presence on TikTok with 128,000 followers.
Denyard said: “Waitrose as a brand punches well above its weight in food culture. We have the fastest growing channel for food in the UK.”
He said the retailer was thinking carefully about how to ensure it kept the trust it had gained from food fans. “We want to do it in a way that’s right for the community that we’re part of.”

Denyard, who joined Waitrose in January after four years leading Tesco’s online business, wants to link Waitrose stores and the digital world more closely with a host of ideas including AI assistants for staff and shoppers.

Staff across the chain are now equipped with handheld gadgets that give them access to AI-assisted information. The Rosie system, which began trials last year and is now in most shops, can help staff provide advice on suitable wines for different meals, and where in store to find products.

Denyard says the introduction of electronic pricing labels in almost all its shops over the past year will, from this week, also help staff, including those picking shelves for online orders, to find products. Rosie will indicate product locations with a flashing light on the electronic shelf label.
The system is said to have freed up thousands of hours of staff time, amid pressure to cut costs as a result of higher minimum wages and tax.
After opening two supermarkets this year, its first in eight years, Waitrose is to open as many as six new outlets of various sizes in 2027 as part of a £1bn investment plan.

Despite industry chatter about consolidation, Denyard says Waitrose is not looking to buy a rival chain. But in the event of a widely expected move by the UK’s second biggest supermarket chain, Sainsbury’s, to buy up either Asda or Morrisons, or any attempts by rivals to downsize, Waitrose will be waiting in the wings to pick up store locations.
“We will remain acquisitive and we are keen to make sure that we’re at the table taking those opportunities,” he said.

Next year’s plans include a supermarket in Oakham, Rutland, and three convenience shops in Bedminster inBristol, Chalk Farm in London and Springstead Village in Cambridge, as well as refurbishing 29 existing branches.

Denyard says he is keen for more larger supermarkets, such as those recently opened in Hale Barns and Cricklewood in north London, where the company can show off its full foodie credentials with fresh food counters, something removed by most rivals.

Waitrose, which has more than 300 supermarkets, is introducing meat, fish and sushi counters, on-site bakeries and fine wine sections in more stores. It is also using pop-ups, such as a mini cheese tasting table in Hale Barns.
Denyard says counters are “a core part of our offer” as the foodies Waitrose wants to attract “really want to shop them”.

Those foodies are also being courted with an ever-expanding own-label range, particularly at the premium end with Waitrose No.1. Sales of the luxury own brand are growing by more than 10% year on year despite the squeeze on household budgets, as many buy ready meals instead of takeaways and dining out.
Denyard says there is “lots of headroom” to expand the range and that own-label is a key part of what makes Waitrose distinctive.

After a difficult period, when sales were hit by IT problems that led to gaps on shelves, Waitrose is holding market share, according to the latest figures from the market analysts Worldpanel by Numerator. It is coming under pressure from Marks & Spencer, however, which has a higher share of the grocery market by some measures after opening a number of new food-led outlets.

Denyard nonetheless says Waitrose is “resilient and competitive in the market”. “Customers have a repertoire of places that they go for different missions and fulfil different needs across the course of a given week or month,” he said. “Our job is to make sure in that mix we are brilliantly differentiated and give food lovers more reasons to come to Waitrose, and we feel like we’re getting well down the path.”
